q: (S)-2-Bromopentane is treated with NaSCH3 in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Thiolate is a strong nucleophile and a weak base, and DMF is polar aprotic. What happens to the configuration in that mechanism?
w: CH3S− is an excellent nucleophile but a weak base, so this secondary bromide reacts by SN2: backside attack with inversion at C2. Priorities in the product are SCH3 > propyl > CH3 > H, the same pattern as Br > propyl > CH3 > H in the reactant, so inversion changes the label: (R)-2-(methylthio)pentane.
x: This is the (S) product, formed with retention. SN2 goes by backside attack and inverts the stereocenter.
C has SCH<sub>3</sub> on C3. S<sub>N</sub>2 has no carbocation and no shift; the nucleophile bonds to the carbon that held Br.
This is an E2 alkene. Thiolates are weak bases, so elimination is minor with this secondary bromide.

q: (R)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is warmed in methanol. What is the stereochemical outcome for the substitution product, 3-methoxy-3-methylhexane?
h: Which mechanism does a tertiary bromide follow in a weakly nucleophilic protic solvent? What is the shape of its intermediate?
w: A tertiary bromide in methanol reacts by SN1. Ionization gives a planar (sp2) tertiary carbocation, and methanol can add to either face, so both enantiomers form: a racemic (or nearly racemic) mixture. In practice a small excess of inversion is often seen because the departing Br− briefly shields the front face (ion pairing), but the product is essentially racemized.
x: Clean inversion is the S<sub>N</sub>2 outcome. A tertiary carbon is too hindered for backside attack.
Retention would need the nucleophile to approach only the face the bromide left; a planar cation has two equally open faces.
The product has a single stereocenter, so it cannot be meso; meso compounds need two or more stereocenters and an internal mirror plane.

q: (2R,3R)-2-Bromo-3-methylpentane reacts with NaN3 in DMSO. Which product forms?
h: Only one stereocenter is touched by the nucleophile. What happens there, and what happens at the other one?
w: Azide in DMSO is a strong nucleophile and weak base, so the reaction is SN2 at C2: backside attack inverts C2. N3 takes the top priority that Br had, so the C2 label flips from R to S. C3 is not involved, and its substituent priorities (C2 branch > ethyl > CH3 > H) are unchanged, so it stays R: (2S,3R). It is a diastereomer of the retention product.
x: This is retention at C2, which would need frontside attack. S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts the carbon that is attacked.
C3 is not attacked and no bond to it breaks, so its configuration (and label) stays R; inverting both gives the enantiomer of the retention product.
This keeps C2 and inverts C3, the wrong carbon. The reaction occurs at C2, which bears the bromine.

q: cis-1-Bromo-4-methylcyclohexane is treated with NaN3 in DMSO. What is the major product?
c: a 1:1 mixture of the cis and trans azides
h: Backside attack puts the nucleophile on the opposite face of the ring from where the leaving group was.
w: Azide/DMSO gives SN2. The nucleophile enters from the face opposite the C–Br bond, so the azide ends up on the opposite face of the ring from the original bromine. The bromide was cis to the methyl, so the azide is trans: trans-1-azido-4-methylcyclohexane.
x: This is the cis azide, the retention product. Backside attack moves the substituent to the other face of the ring.
This is 4-methylcyclohexene, the E2 product. Azide is a weak base, so elimination is minor.
A cis/trans mixture would come from a planar carbocation (S<sub>N</sub>1). Azide in DMSO with a secondary bromide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: The tosylate shown is treated with NaSCH<sub>3</sub> in DMF. What is the major product?
h: Tosylate is an excellent leaving group; thiolate is a strong nucleophile and weak base. Track which carbon changes and which does not.
w: SN2 at the carbon bearing OTs inverts that carbon only; the carbon bearing CH3 is untouched. The starting (1R,2R) tosylate has OTs and CH3 trans; after inversion SCH3 and CH3 are cis, with the methyl-bearing carbon still in its original configuration: A.
x: B keeps the trans relationship, i.e., retention at the carbon attacked. SN2 inverts.
This is cis, but it is the enantiomer of A: the methyl-bearing carbon has also been inverted, and no bond to that carbon is made or broken.
D comes from a carbocation and hydride shift (S<sub>N</sub>1). A strong nucleophile in DMF reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 without rearrangement.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Which step breaks the C–O bond, and which only changes the oxygen?
w: Step 1 converts the OH into OTs. The C–O bond is not broken (the oxygen attacks sulfur), so the tosylate keeps the (R) configuration. Step 2 is SN2 by cyanide with inversion. In the nitrile, C≡N (C attached to N,N,N) > ethyl > CH3, the same priority pattern as the alcohol, so inversion gives (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: This is the (R) nitrile: net retention. Only the cyanide step touches the stereocenter, and it inverts.
This is the tosylate intermediate, the product of step 1 only. Cyanide then displaces the tosylate.
Racemization would need a carbocation. Cyanide in DMSO with a secondary tosylate reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q:
(R)-Butan-2-ol is converted to 2-methylbutanenitrile by two routes.
Route 1: 1. PBr3 2. NaCN, DMSO
Route 2: 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaCN, DMSO
Which statement about the products is correct?
h: Count inversions. Does PBr<sub>3</sub> break the C–O bond? Does TsCl?
w: PBr3 activates the OH and Br− then displaces it by SN2: inversion, giving (S)-2-bromobutane. Cyanide inverts again, so route 1 shows two inversions = net retention: (R) nitrile. TsCl makes the tosylate without touching the C–O bond (retention); cyanide then inverts once: (S) nitrile. Priorities are OH/Br/CN > ethyl > CH3 throughout, so each inversion flips the label. Route 1 → (R), route 2 → (S).
x: PBr<sub>3</sub> is not a retention reagent like TsCl; the bromide forms by S<sub>N</sub>2 with inversion, so route 1 has two inversions.
Tosylation leaves the stereocenter unchanged, so route 2 has only one inversion and gives (S), not (R).
This swaps the two routes: the PBr<sub>3</sub> route has two inversions (net retention), the TsCl route only one.

q: (S)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with SOCl2 in pyridine. What is the product?
h: In pyridine, the chlorosulfite intermediate is attacked by free chloride. From which side?
w: SOCl2 turns the OH into a chlorosulfite (–OS(O)Cl), an excellent leaving group. With pyridine present, free Cl− attacks from the back (SN2), giving inversion. Cl > propyl > CH3, like OH > propyl > CH3, so the label flips: (R)-2-chloropentane.
x: This is the retention product. Retention is seen with SOCl<sub>2</sub> alone (no pyridine) in some cases; with pyridine the chloride attacks from the back.
C, 3-chloropentane, would require a carbocation and hydride shift. The pyridine conditions avoid a free carbocation.
Racemization requires an S<sub>N</sub>1 carbocation. SOCl<sub>2</sub>/pyridine on a secondary alcohol goes by S<sub>N</sub>2.

q: (R)-Pentan-2-ol is treated with TsCl in pyridine. What is the configuration of the tosylate formed?
c: (R), because the C–O bond is not broken
(S), because tosylation is an SN2 reaction at carbon
(S), because the priority of OTs is lower than that of OH
h: In tosylation, which atom does the alcohol oxygen attack?
w: The alcohol oxygen attacks the sulfur of TsCl and displaces chloride from sulfur; pyridine removes the proton. Nothing happens at the stereocenter: the C–O bond stays intact, and OTs (O attached) still has top priority. The tosylate is (R), with retention. Inversion comes only later, when a nucleophile displaces the tosylate.
x: The substitution in this step happens at sulfur, not at the stereocenter. The carbon is untouched.
No carbocation forms: the C–O bond does not break during tosylation.
OTs is attached through oxygen, just like OH, so it keeps the highest priority; the label does not change.

q: (S)-5-Bromohexan-1-amine is warmed in dilute solution. A cyclic amine forms. What is it?
h: Count the ring atoms: the nitrogen plus every carbon from C1 to the carbon that bears Br. Then decide what happens at that carbon.
w: The amine nitrogen attacks C5 intramolecularly. The ring contains N, C1, C2, C3, C4 and C5: six atoms, a piperidine with the C6 methyl on the carbon next to N. Intramolecular SN2 is backside attack, so C5 is inverted. N replaces Br as the top priority (N > ring CH2 > CH3), so (S) becomes (R)-2-methylpiperidine. Dilute solution favors ring closure over intermolecular reaction.
x: This is (S)-2-methylpiperidine, the retention product. The nitrogen must approach from the back of the C–Br bond.
This is a five-membered ring, which would need N to bond to C4, a carbon with no leaving group.
This is an elimination product. A neutral amine is a weak base, and ring closure to a six-membered ring is fast.

q: 4-Chlorobutan-1-ol is treated with NaH in DMF. What is the major organic product?
h: NaH removes the O–H proton. The alkoxide can now reach the carbon that holds Cl. How big is that ring?
w: NaH deprotonates the alcohol. The alkoxide attacks C4 from the back in an intramolecular SN2 (an intramolecular Williamson synthesis). The ring contains O, C1, C2, C3 and C4: five atoms, so the product is tetrahydrofuran. Five-membered rings close fastest.
x: This is a six-membered ring, one atom too many; there are only four carbons between O and Cl, counting both ends.
This is a four-membered ring (oxetane); it would need the alkoxide to attack C3, which has no leaving group.
This is an elimination product. The alkoxide finds the nearby carbon intramolecularly far faster than it removes a β-hydrogen from a primary chloride.

q: Two stereoisomers of 2-chlorocyclohexanol (each racemic) are treated with NaOH. Only one gives cyclohexene oxide rapidly. Which one, and why?
c: I (trans), because O− and Cl can both be axial, anti to each other, for backside attack
II (cis), because O− and Cl are on the same face and close together
I (trans), because its O− is equatorial and attacks the front of the C–Cl bond
II (cis), because its more stable chair puts Cl axial
h: Epoxide formation is an intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2. Where must the nucleophile be relative to the C–Cl bond?
w: Ring closure is an intramolecular SN2, so the alkoxide must reach the back of the C–Cl bond. In the trans isomer, a ring flip puts OH and Cl both axial, pointing in opposite directions (anti-periplanar); the O− then sits directly behind the C–Cl bond and closes the epoxide quickly. In the cis isomer one group is always axial and the other equatorial, so the O− can never reach the backside. Answer: I, the trans isomer.
x: Being on the same face is exactly wrong for S<sub>N</sub>2; the alkoxide would attack the front of the C–Cl bond.
An S<sub>N</sub>2 nucleophile must attack the back of the C–Cl bond, which requires the diaxial (anti) arrangement, not frontside attack.
An axial Cl alone is not enough; in the cis isomer the O<sup>−</sup> is then equatorial and points away from the backside of the C–Cl bond.

q: (2R,3S)-3-Bromobutan-2-ol is treated with aqueous NaOH. What is the major product?
h: Deprotonated OH attacks the neighboring C–Br carbon from the back. Which carbon is inverted and which keeps its configuration?
w: The alkoxide at C2 attacks C3 from the back (intramolecular SN2), closing an epoxide. C2 keeps its configuration (its C–O bond is not broken); C3 is inverted. Working this through gives the trans-epoxide (2R,3R)-2,3-dimethyloxirane. The intramolecular reaction is much faster than attack by external hydroxide.
x: This is cis-2,3-dimethyloxirane (meso). It would require retention at C3, i.e., frontside attack.
This is the (2S,3S) enantiomer of the product; it would require inverting C2 as well, but no bond to C2 is broken.
This is the diol from intermolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 by HO<sup>−</sup>. With an alkoxide held right next to the C–Br carbon, ring closure wins.

q: The single stereoisomer of 1-chloro-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane shown is heated in methanol. Which statement describes the substitution products?
c: A mixture of both ring stereoisomers of 1-methoxy-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane
Only the stereoisomer with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the face opposite where Cl was
Only the stereoisomer with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the same face where Cl was
h: A tertiary chloride in methanol forms a carbocation. Can the nucleophile reach both faces of it?
w: The tertiary chloride ionizes (SN1) to a planar carbocation at C1. Methanol can add to the top or bottom face, so OCH3 ends up either cis or trans to the C4 methyl: a mixture of both stereoisomers. (The ratio need not be 1:1, since the two faces of the ring cation are not equivalent, but both form.)
x: Exclusive inversion is the S<sub>N</sub>2 result; a tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back.
A planar cation has no memory of which face the chloride left from, so retention alone is not expected.
The cation at C1 is already tertiary; a hydride shift to C2 would make a less stable secondary cation, and no rearrangement is favored.

q: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated HBr. What is the major alkyl bromide?
h: A secondary alcohol in strong acid loses water. Is the resulting cation the most stable one available?
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 gives a tertiary cation, which Br− captures (SN1): 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
x: This is the unrearranged bromide. The secondary cation rearranges to the adjacent tertiary site faster than bromide traps it.
C would need the cation at a primary carbon; shifts go toward more stable cations.
This is the E1 alkene, which is not an alkyl bromide; with concentrated HBr, bromide capture gives the substitution product.

h: You need a way to turn OH into a leaving group that bromide displaces directly, without forming a carbocation.
w: PBr3 converts the OH into an –OPBr2 leaving group, and bromide displaces it by SN2 (with inversion). No carbocation forms, so no hydride shift occurs: PBr3.
x: HBr protonates the OH and water leaves to give a secondary cation, which shifts to the tertiary cation: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
NaBr/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates HBr in situ, so it gives the same carbocation and the same rearrangement.
Without activation, HO<sup>−</sup> is far too poor a leaving group; bromide in DMSO does not react with the alcohol.

q: Butan-1-ol reacts with concentrated HBr to give 1-bromobutane. Which statement about the mechanism is correct?
c: Br<sup>−</sup> displaces water from the protonated alcohol in one step (S<sub>N</sub>2)
The protonated alcohol loses water to form a primary carbocation, which Br<sup>−</sup> traps
Br<sup>−</sup> displaces hydroxide directly from the neutral alcohol
The primary cation rearranges to the 2-butyl cation before Br<sup>−</sup> adds
h: Which leaving group is present after protonation? Can a primary carbocation form?
w: Strong acid first protonates the OH, converting the very poor leaving group HO− into neutral H2O. A primary cation is too unstable to form, so Br− attacks the CH2 from the back as water departs: SN2 on the protonated alcohol. That is why 1-bromobutane is obtained without rearrangement.
x: A primary carbocation is too high in energy to form under these conditions; primary alcohols react with HBr by S<sub>N</sub>2.
Hydroxide is a strong base and a very poor leaving group; the alcohol must be protonated first.
No free primary cation forms, so there is nothing to rearrange; the product is 1-bromobutane, not 2-bromobutane.
